transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-27 10:00 PT, Duration 62 min. Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Verdant Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Verdant SRE), Elena Park (Verdant Finance).

Auto-summary (auto): Quick sync to validate pilot health, align on pilot-to-prod gating criteria, and agree on bench runs.

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then we'll dig into the stability numbers. Maya, Tom, Elena you there?
[00:06] Maya: Yep here, hi Ava. Hi Liam.
[00:08] Tom: Tom here.
[00:09] Elena: Elena, yes.
[00:11] Liam: Liam on the line, thanks.

[00:20] Ava: Cool. So agenda — usage & cost anomalies we saw last week, latency tail spikes during bursts, quick security Qs about VPC and KMS, and then propose a 72-hour stability run on dedicated capacity. Any other asks before we dive?
[00:31] Maya: Nope that's good. Main ask is: if we scale to 2x traffic can you guarantee sub 200 ms median and 99.9th under 1.5s? That's our customer SLA target.

[00:45] Liam: Got it. Quick context: on our hosted fleet we hit medians around 120 ms for the tuned model but we've seen occasional tail events hitting 1.8 to 2.2 seconds when prefix cache miss coincided with GC cycles on a particular node. We're pretty sure those were node-level noise and a routing policy tweak fixed the immediate issue.

[01:05] Tom: Right, we observed that in our logs too. We saw spikes around 03:00 UTC tied to daily batch jobs, weirdly. Could be thundering herd from webhook retries.

[01:18] Maya: Also to call out, our token mix changed after the new summarization feature launched — avg sequence length increased from 120 to 240, which likely increases per-token CPU/GPU time. We didn't want to be charged twice because of this unexpected shift.

[01:34] Elena: And finance side — we got a surprise invoice bump last month, not huge but enough to trigger a review. Can you walk through cost levers again? We want predictable forecasts.

[01:44] Ava: Totally. Quick on cost levers: batching settings, prefix/KV cache, model quantization profile, and dedicated vs hosted routing. For forecasts we can provide token-level burn projections and what-if scenarios. We'll include a cost sensitivity sheet in the SOW.

[01:58] Liam: To be specific on the stability tangent — for the 99.9th percentile we generally recommend Dedicated capacity with pinned GPU pools for production. Hosted can be configured with higher priority routing but you lose strict isolation. Dedicated reduces cross-tenant noisy neighbor risks and gives predictable latency and throughput.

[02:14] Maya: So Dedicated sounds fine, but we need private network. Do you support VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for key wrapping? Also we have a requirement for audit logs retention for 13 months.

[02:28] Ava: Yes on both. For private deployments we can do VPC peering or PrivateLink depending on cloud. Customer-managed KMS is supported via our KMS integration and for Private (on-prem/VPC) you can bring your own KMS/HSM. Audit logs retention is configurable — longer retention is an add-on but we can include an enterprise clause for 13 months in the SOW.

[02:46] Elena: Good. That helps. Back to the cost bump — can you explain where the extra tokens came from; is it sequence length shift or is there a hidden retry loop causing duplicate calls?

[02:58] Tom: We did see retry storms earlier in July because the service returning 429 had a client retry with no jitter. We paused that client but wanted Redwood to confirm if dedupe at the ingress is possible.

[03:10] Liam: We have dedupe patterns at the routing layer but we don't automatically dedupe identical request payloads by default — that's an opt-in caching layer concerned with idempotency semantics. For safety we suggest client-side jitter and token-based idempotency keys, but we can enable prefix caching to cut duplicate token spend for repeated prefixes.

[03:30] Maya: Prefix caching — does that work across sessions? Our UX uses context windows with user history, so prefixes vary.

[03:36] Liam: Good q. Prefix caching helps when you have repeated prompt scaffolding, like a system prompt or instructions reused across users. If user history differs, caching hit rates fall. We can measure expected hit-rate if you share the 7-day sample of prompts and sequences — that's one of the next steps.

[03:50] Ava: Right, Tom we'll take that traffic CSV. Also we propose a 72-hour run on a dedicated pool that mirrors your 95th percentile load scaled to 2x for headroom, that'll give us more confidence on tail behavior.

[04:05] Tom: Sounds reasonable — what metrics will you collect? We'll need flame graphs and kernel-level traces if things go sideways.

[04:12] Liam: We'll push logs for latency distribution, GPU utilization, KV cache hit/miss ratio, and per-token timing. For deeper analysis we'll collaborate on perf profiles and can provide pprof-like artifacts and flamegraphs. Note — for privacy we'll scrub any PII from logs.

[04:28] Elena: Are there any risk items that would push this over budget? Like per-hour GPU surcharges for dedicated burst usage or storage for audit logs?

[04:36] Ava: There are two cost buckets to watch: sustained dedicated capacity commit vs burstable overage rates; and audit/log retention storage. We'll model both. The SOW will show cost at listed commit level and projected overage at X% traffic variance.

[04:50] Maya: On the reliability gating criteria to move pilot to prod: we want 30 days with no more than 3 P99 incidents, median under 200 ms, and sustained error rate under 0.2%. Is that realistic?

[05:02] Liam: It's aggressive but doable with dedicated capacity and the routing rules we'll set. The tricky part is the long tails caused by cache churn or large sequence requests. We'll set up guardrails: cap single-request tokens, autoscale thresholds, and fallbacks to a slightly smaller model if the primary is overloaded.

[05:21] Tom: Fallbacks — will that affect output quality? We don't want regressions in summarization quality for customer-facing flows.

[05:26] Liam: We can define A/B fallback policies with a quality monitor. If the primary model crosses latency thresholds, traffic splits to a quantized or slightly smaller model and we surface a degraded-quality flag. We'll also run automated evals on a holdout prompt set to ensure quality doesn't drop below an agreed threshold.

[05:44] Maya: Ok that works. Question on SSO and RBAC: we need SAML 2.0, SCIM provisioning and role-based controls for different teams. Also session access logs for investigators.

[05:55] Ava: We support SAML and SCIM; RBAC is configurable in the console. Session access logs are part of audit logs — we'll show how to stream to your SIEM or export them. We'll attach the network diagram and admin flows in the doc pack.

[06:10] Elena: Please include estimated cost impact for SCIM/SSO support? Is there an extra license fee?

[06:15] Ava: Core SSO/SCIM is included in Enterprise tier; if you want dedicated support or extended seat provisioning automation that's an add-on. We'll call that out in the pricing sheet.

[06:25] Maya: One more perf ask — during earlier spike we saw a 15% drop in throughput when multiple long-context requests ran concurrently. Is there a per-request concurrency cap we can set?

[06:36] Liam: Yes you can set concurrency limits per API key and per-route. Also batching strategy impacts this: continuous batching can improve throughput but raises tail latencies for tiny requests. We'll help tune batching window to your mix.

[06:50] Tom: For the 72-hour run can Redwood simulate a mix of short and long requests? We'll provide the distribution.

[06:56] Liam: Absolutely — we can replay synthetic traffic matching the profile and run with the same autoscale policies you plan to use.

[07:05] Ava: Ok summarizing next steps: Ava sends SOW + pricing + security pack by 2026-09-01; Tom sends traffic CSV by 2026-08-31; Liam kicks off 72-hour dedicated run and shares logs by 2026-09-03. Any blockers?

[07:20] Maya: No blockers. One ask: include a short runbook for incident escalation with Redwood oncall contact and expected SLAs for support.

[07:28] Ava: Will do.

[07:32] [crosstalk] Tom: also can we have a post-run review meeting — 30-45 min?
[07:36] Ava: Yup schedule for the week after the run. I'll propose two windows.

[07:40] Elena: Great. Finance will review SOW and likely ok the committed capacity if the cost model looks stable.

[07:47] Ava: Perfect, thanks all. We'll follow up via email with attachments. End.

Auto-action-items (auto): see action_items above. Notes about transcription: occasional mis-hears on acronyms, e.g., KMS transcribed as K-M-S or KMZ in some snippets. End of transcript.
